title: Look Twice Before You Answer: Memory-Space Visual Retracing for Hallucination Mitigation in Multimodal Large Language Models

raw.stage1:
### Purpose:
The contribution's purpose is to mitigate hallucinations in multimodal large language models (MLLMs) without relying on external knowledge retrieval or additional fine-tuning. Papers [2], [3], [5], [11], [15], and [20] all address hallucination mitigation in MLLMs or LVLMs, but they rely on methods such as instruction tuning, retrieval augmentation, or contrastive decoding. None of these papers explicitly target hallucination mitigation without external knowledge retrieval or fine-tuning. Therefore, the specific purpose of this contribution is **not covered**.

### Mechanism:
The mechanism, MEMVR (Memory-space Visual Retracing), uses visual tokens as supplementary evidence and re-injects them into the model via feed-forward networks (FFNs) acting as "key-value memory" during intermediate layers. Papers [6], [7], [22], [23], and [27] discuss key-value memory mechanisms in various contexts, including person re-identification, question answering, efficient transformer decoding, and feed-forward layers as key-value memories. The primitive of using FFNs as key-value memory is covered by [23], which explicitly identifies feed-forward layers in transformers as operating as key-value memories. Thus, the mechanism is **covered**.

### Evaluation:
The evaluation involves testing the method on multiple MLLMs (LLaVA-1.5-7B, Qwen-VL-Chat, GLM4V) and seven benchmark categories, with GPT-4o used for assessment. Papers [5], [11], [15], and [20] evaluate hallucination mitigation methods on LVLMs using similar benchmark families and metrics, such as visual contrastive decoding and instruction contrastive decoding. The use of GPT-based evaluation (e.g., GPT-4) is also common in prior work, such as [19]. Since the evaluation design (benchmark family and metric semantics) is reused, the evaluation is **covered**.

### Domain:
The domain is multimodal large language models (MLLMs) and hallucination mitigation. Papers [2], [3], [5], [11], [15], and [20] all operate in the same general application area of hallucination mitigation in MLLMs or LVLMs. Although the specific models and datasets differ, the domain is **covered**.

## Purpose

The contribution aims to mitigate hallucinations in MLLMs (asserting content not present in images) without external knowledge retrieval or additional fine-tuning.

Papers [2], [3], [5], [15], [20] all address hallucination mitigation in MLLMs/LVLMs in a training-free manner without external retrieval. Paper [5] (VCD) explicitly introduces a "simple and training-free method" to mitigate object hallucinations in LVLMs. Paper [3] addresses hallucinations in LVLMs without retrieval. Paper [2] introduces a "training-free" approach for MLLM hallucinations. The purpose is clearly covered.

## Mechanism

The core mechanism is re-injecting visual tokens as supplementary evidence through FFN layers (treated as key-value memory) at intermediate trigger layers — plug-and-play, architecture-agnostic, single-pass inference.

Paper [23] ("Transformer Feed-Forward Layers Are Key-Value Memories") directly establishes that "feed-forward layers in transformer-based language models operate as key-value memories, where each key correlates with textual patterns." This is the foundational primitive being exploited. However, the contribution's mechanism goes further: it uses this FFN-as-memory insight to *re-inject visual tokens* at intermediate layers to correct hallucination. Paper [8] discusses visual token behavior in MLLMs and notes that visual information is absorbed in early layers. Paper [12] uses inter-layer contrastive decoding by comparing internal layers. None of the prior papers combine the FFN-as-key-value-memory primitive with visual token re-injection at intermediate layers for hallucination mitigation. Paper [23] covers the key-value memory interpretation of FFN, but the specific mechanism of retracing/re-injecting visual tokens through FFN memory to mitigate hallucination is not present in any prior paper. The closest is [23] for the FFN-as-memory primitive, but the re-injection of visual tokens as the corrective mechanism is absent.

Actually, re-examining: the mechanism primitive is "re-inject input tokens (visual) as supplementary evidence into intermediate FFN layers." Paper [23] covers the FFN-as-KV-memory framing. But the act of re-injecting visual tokens mid-inference to correct output is not covered. No prior paper uses this specific primitive. NONE for mechanism.

## Evaluation

The evaluation uses multiple MLLMs (LLaVA-1.5-7B, Qwen-VL-Chat, GLM4V), seven benchmark types, GPT-4o as judge, and comparison against VCD/OPERA contrastive decoding baselines with inference time analysis.

Papers [2], [3], [5], [15], [20] all evaluate on MLLM hallucination benchmarks (CHAIR, POPE, MME, etc.) with similar setups comparing against VCD/OPERA. Paper [5] uses CHAIR and POPE benchmarks. Paper [20] compares against VCD and OPERA. The evaluation design (multi-MLLM evaluation on standard hallucination benchmarks, LLM-as-judge, comparison with contrastive decoding baselines) is clearly covered by these prior papers.

## Domain

The domain is multimodal large language models / hallucination mitigation. Papers [2], [3], [5], [8], [11], [15], [20] all operate in this exact domain.

### Purpose
The contribution's purpose is to trigger visual redrawing in multimodal large language models (LVLMs) when the model exhibits uncertainty in visual memory and provide a theoretical basis for this approach. Several prior papers address hallucination mitigation in LVLMs, but none explicitly focus on triggering visual redrawing based on uncertainty. Papers like [2], [3], [5], [8], and [10] aim to mitigate hallucinations in LVLMs, but their objectives differ in that they focus on penalizing hallucinated tokens, instruction tuning, or fine-grained feedback rather than uncertainty-triggered visual redrawing. Thus, no prior paper shares the same purpose.

### Mechanism
The mechanism involves a dynamic premature layer injection strategy, where visual redrawing is triggered based on the entropy (uncertainty) of layer outputs, and information-theoretic reasoning is used to prove that visual redrawing reduces hallucinations. Paper [7] discusses early exit strategies based on confidence levels, and [15], [16], [19], and [25] explore early-exit mechanisms in various contexts, including LVLMs. However, none of these papers use entropy-based uncertainty to trigger visual redrawing or provide an information-theoretic proof of its effectiveness. Paper [14] and [21] discuss uncertainty quantification, but they focus on Bayesian methods or last-layer uncertainty estimation rather than dynamic layer injection based on entropy. Thus, no prior paper shares the same mechanism.

### Evaluation
The evaluation primarily involves qualitative/theoretical proof, supplemented by uncertainty analysis (e.g., entropy distribution of early-exit layer outputs in LLaVA-1.5-7B). Papers [7], [15], [16], [19], and [25] use early-exit evaluations, but their designs focus on efficiency or accuracy trade-offs rather than uncertainty analysis. Paper [14] and [21] evaluate uncertainty quantification methods, but their designs differ from the entropy-based uncertainty analysis used here. No prior paper uses the same evaluation design.

### Domain
The domain is multimodal large language models (LVLMs). Papers [2], [3], [5], [6], [8], [10], [20], and [24] all address hallucination mitigation in LVLMs, making the domain covered.

## PURPOSE: "让视觉重描在模型对视觉记忆不确定时被触发，并给出理论依据"
(Trigger visual re-description when the model is uncertain about visual memory, with theoretical justification)

The purpose is to adaptively trigger a visual grounding/re-description mechanism based on model uncertainty, specifically to reduce hallucinations in MLLMs. Paper [2] (ESREAL) aims to suppress hallucinations via semantic reconstruction in VLMs — but it doesn't focus on uncertainty-triggered activation. Paper [3] (LURE) mitigates object hallucination but through post-hoc revision, not uncertainty-triggered re-description. Paper [9] (DiLa) dynamically selects internal layers to mitigate hallucinations in LLMs, but doesn't involve visual re-description triggered by uncertainty. No prior paper specifically pursues the objective of "trigger visual re-description when uncertainty is high AND provide theoretical justification for why this reduces hallucination." The closest is [2] (semantic reconstruction to mitigate hallucination) but the uncertainty-triggered adaptive mechanism is absent. No paper covers this specific purpose.

## MECHANISM: "动态早熟层注入策略（dynamic premature layer injection）：按各层输出不确定性（熵）触发视觉重描；并从信息论视角理论证明视觉重描能降低幻觉"

The mechanism combines: (1) entropy-based uncertainty measurement at intermediate layers, (2) using that entropy to trigger visual re-description injection, (3) information-theoretic proof. 

Paper [12] (DoLa) contrasts logits from earlier vs. later layers to reduce hallucinations — uses premature layer outputs but via contrastive decoding, not entropy-triggered injection. Paper [9] (DiLa) "dynamically selects appropriate internal layers" for contrastive decoding — closer, but still contrastive decoding, not entropy-triggered visual re-description. Paper [7], [15], [16], [19], [23], [25] all use early exit with confidence/entropy thresholds to decide when to exit — the entropy-based triggering at intermediate layers is present, but the triggered action is "exit" not "inject visual re-description." None of these combine entropy-triggered intermediate-layer detection with visual re-description injection plus information-theoretic proof. The specific primitive of "use layer-wise entropy to trigger visual context re-injection" is not covered.

## EVALUATION: "定性/理论证明；不确定性分析（32层LLaVA-1.5-7B，早退层输出分布不确定性）；消融显示动态重描优于固定层"

The evaluation design includes: uncertainty analysis of intermediate layer outputs in a specific MLLM, and ablation comparing dynamic vs. fixed layer strategies. Paper [12] (DoLa) analyzes layer-wise output distributions to motivate their method. Paper [9] (DiLa) performs layer selection analysis. Papers [7], [15], [16], [19], [25] use early-exit with confidence/entropy analysis across layers. The ablation design (dynamic vs. fixed layer comparison) is a generic substitution experiment. The uncertainty analysis of intermediate layers in LLMs/MLLMs appears in [12] and [9]. The evaluation design of analyzing per-layer entropy distributions and ablating dynamic vs. fixed strategies is substantively covered by [12] and [9].

## DOMAIN: "多模态大语言模型"

Papers [2], [3], [5], [6], [8], [10], [20], [24] all work in multimodal large language models / vision-language models. This domain is clearly covered.
